world_behind.title: A dead king's law is the first thing tested
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says Mosiah left none to reign in his stead, then adds that he had established laws, that the people had acknowledged them, and that they were therefore obliged to abide by them. Thirteen verses later Alma sentences a man to death by "the law which has been given us by Mosiah, our last king." The new order's first act is to enforce the old one.

world_behind.title: The clock has changed
world_behind.text: The book opens in the first year of the reign of the judges and closes in the fifth. Every date from here to the end of Nephite history counts from the vacancy the previous chapter created, and the phrase "from this time forward" is in the opening sentence.

world_behind.title: The hill Manti enters the record here
world_behind.text: Nehor is carried to the top of it and dies there, and this is the first time the name is written down. It goes on to attach to a land, a city, a valley and a river through the whole war section of the book. The map of the next forty chapters begins with an execution site.

world_behind.title: Nehor's platform is a payroll question
world_behind.text: He preaches that every priest and teacher ought to become popular, ought not to labor with their hands, and ought to be supported by the people. Noah's priests had lived exactly that way on taxes, and Alma's own church at the waters of Mormon had forbidden it in as many words.

world_behind.title: The man he kills is somebody
world_behind.text: Gideon drew his sword and swore to kill king Noah, and later planned the escape that got Limhi's people out of Lamanite hands. The record stops in verse 8 to say so, then kills him in verse 9, "stricken with many years."

world_behind.title: The charge is cited and left undefined
world_behind.text: Nephi had set out what priestcraft was two volumes earlier: men preaching and setting themselves up for a light to get gain and the praise of the world, not seeking the welfare of Zion. Alma uses the word in court the way a lawyer names a statute, as something the room is assumed to know.

world_behind.title: Two legal systems, running side by side
world_behind.text: Mosiah's law punishes acts: lying, theft, robbery, murder. Verse 33 has it enforced on every man who transgressed it. The church runs a second code entirely: a strict rule against its own members persecuting anyone (v. 21), enforced by blotting names out of a register (v. 24). One takes lives; the other takes membership.

words.text: The chair, standing for the office. Every earlier use in the record is God's seat or Christ's. That is the seat where the unclean cannot stand, where all men must appear, where Enos hopes to meet many souls spotless. Here it is furniture in Zarahemla, and from this verse forward the record dates its years by who is sitting in it.

Preaching for pay. The singular form appears twice in scripture and both are in this chapter; everywhere else the word is plural. The singular makes it an act. That is what a charge in a courtroom has to be.

Shameful, disgracing. The word is unique in scripture, and what it describes is the manner of Nehor's death rather than its method. The verse spends its detail on the acknowledgment he made between the heavens and the earth, and then disposes of the execution in three words.

Dared. It appears four times in this chapter out of thirty-eight in the record, always negated and always attached to what the law would do. They durst not lie, durst not steal, durst not rob, durst not commit any wickedness if it were known. The chapter's account of public order is a list of things people did not dare.

Heatedly, with heat. Members of the church "began to contend warmly with their adversaries, even unto blows." The adverb is unique in scripture, and the sentence gets from temperature to fists inside a single clause.

Home-made, domestic, in the older sense rather than the modern one about appearance. It is unique in scripture and it ends an inventory of imports and luxuries: silk, fine-twined linen, and all manner of good homely cloth. The last item on the list is the one they wove themselves.

Thirsty. The prospering church sends away nobody naked, hungry, athirst, sick, or unnourished. The word appears once more in this record, three chapters later, in the list of people the proud were turning their backs on.

phrases.text: Paul's charge to Timothy, spent on a king's obituary. The figure is a soldier's, and the man it describes spent his last year arguing a country out of wanting a king. The phrase appears once in the Bible and once here.

phrases.term: Which he termed to be the word of God
phrases.text: The narrator's verb, slipped between the preaching and its content. Mormon does not write that Nehor preached the word of God; he writes that Nehor called it that. The same construction appears once more in this record (Ammon thinking about those "whom he termed to be his brethren"), and in both places the verb marks a claim the writer is declining to endorse.

phrases.term: All mankind should be saved at the last day
phrases.text: The doctrine that made him popular, and it arrives with three consolations attached: they need not fear, need not tremble, may lift up their heads and rejoice. Nothing in it asks the hearer for anything. Five verses later the man preaching it draws a sword on an old man who argued back.

phrases.term: Was caused, or rather did acknowledge
phrases.text: The record correcting itself inside the sentence. The first verb makes the confession something done to him; the second makes it his own. Mormon writes both and crosses out neither, which leaves the reader holding a question about whether a forced acknowledgment is an acknowledgment.

phrases.term: The law could have no power on any man for his belief
phrases.text: A jurisdictional boundary, stated once in scripture. The clause before it has liars punished and the clause after has thieves punished; belief sits outside the reach of both. The chapter draws the line while describing men it regards as frauds, which is the only time drawing it proves anything.

Isaiah's invitation to come and buy wine and milk, used here as a description of how a persecuted church passed the word around. Nephi and Jacob had both quoted it already. Set against verse 5, where Nehor's hearers "began to support him and give him money," the phrase turns into the chapter's actual dividing line.

phrases.term: The preacher was no better than the hearer
phrases.text: The reply to Nehor's whole platform, reached by way of labor rather than doctrine. The priests left their work to teach, the people left theirs to listen, and everybody went back to work afterward. Both this clause and the "they were all equal" that follows it are unique in scripture.

Two charges joined by an "or" that treats them as interchangeable. The list around them is criminal: whoredoms, robbery, murder. Neither idolatry nor idleness is. Idleness lands in that company because of the chapter's argument about who pays for it.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: A new calendar, and an obligation that outlived its author
verses.text: The year is dated by judges. Mosiah is gone and left nobody on the throne. The verse's "nevertheless" carries the weight: he had made laws, the people had acknowledged them, so the laws stood. A country is described as bound by an agreement.

verses.label: v. 2–6
verses.title: The man, and his three propositions
verses.text: Large, strong, and noted for it. He preaches that priests should be popular, should not work with their hands, and should be paid. Then the sequence: many believed, many gave him money, he grew proud, he bought clothes, he founded a church. Each step is caused by the one before it.

verses.label: v. 7–9
verses.title: Gideon
verses.text: Nehor meets a teacher on the road and contends with him sharply, meaning to draw the church's people away. The man answers him out of the words of God. Then the record names him and gives his history (the deliverer of Limhi's people), and kills him in the next sentence, noting only that he was too old to withstand the blows.

verses.label: v. 10–15
verses.title: Trial, sentence, and a hill
verses.text: He is taken by the people of the church and brought to Alma, and he pleads for himself with much boldness. Alma's charge has two counts: priestcraft, and enforcing it by the sword. The sentence rests on the blood of a righteous man and on a statute nobody has repealed. On the hill Manti he acknowledges, or is made to acknowledge, that what he taught was contrary to the word of God.

verses.label: v. 16–18
verses.title: What the law reached, and what it did not
verses.text: The execution does not stop priestcraft; it only makes it careful. Men went on preaching for riches and honor but pretended to believe what they preached, because liars were punished. They did not steal, rob, or murder either. The paragraph ends by conceding that no law could touch what a man actually believed.

verses.label: v. 19–25
verses.title: Persecution, and a rule the church broke first
verses.text: Those outside the church persecuted those inside it for their humility and for giving the word away free. The church had a strict law forbidding its own members to persecute anyone. Many of them did it anyway, down to fists, and the result was names blotted out and members withdrawing.

verses.label: v. 26–33
verses.title: The counter-portrait
verses.text: Priests who left their labor to teach and returned to it afterward; no man esteemed above his hearers; all equal; substance imparted to the poor by every man according to what he had; no costly apparel; steadiness, then riches, then liberality without respect to persons. Against it, in the last two verses, stand the people outside: sorceries, idleness, babblings, costly apparel, pride, and a law enforced on everyone who broke it.

chapter.title: The second half of the chapter is a point-by-point rebuttal of the first
chapter.text: Nehor's preachers ought not to labor with their hands (v. 3); the church's priests leave their labor and return to it (v. 26). His hearers give him money (v. 5); the church imparts the word without money (v. 20). He wears very costly apparel (v. 6); they do not (v. 27). No argument is made against him after verse 14. The refutation is delivered as a description of somebody else's week.

chapter.title: Priestcraft is described as an economy before it is condemned as a doctrine
chapter.text: What Nehor teaches about salvation occupies one verse. What he teaches about who pays the preacher occupies the rest of his platform, all of his success, and the whole of the chapter's answer. The heresy the record cares about is a compensation scheme.

chapter.title: He is executed for the sword, not for the sermon
chapter.text: Alma names priestcraft first and then says the man is not only guilty of it but has endeavored to enforce it by the sword. The death sentence is pinned to the blood of a righteous man. Three verses later the record puts what a man privately holds outside the reach of any statute at all. The chapter is careful about the distinction at the exact point where blurring it would be easiest and most satisfying.

chapter.title: The church's discipline is aimed at its own side
chapter.text: The strict law in verse 21 forbids members from persecuting outsiders, not the reverse, and verse 22 immediately reports members breaking it. An institution under attack writes its rule about its own conduct and then records its own failure to keep it.

chapter.title: The riches arrive from steadiness, and the chapter stops there
chapter.text: Verse 29 gives the cause plainly: because of the steadiness of the church they began to be exceedingly rich. Verse 30 has them holding it loosely: no respect to persons, in the church or out of it. The usual sequence in this record runs prosperity, pride, fall; here it is interrupted mid-turn, and the fall is left for a later chapter.

chapter.title: "Costly apparel" three times in thirty-three verses
chapter.text: The phrase occurs eight times in the whole record and three of them are here: Nehor buying it, the church declining it, the people outside wearing it. The chapter uses one shopping habit as its index of everything else.

chapter.title: Gideon is identified and then killed without comment
chapter.text: Verse 8 exists only to tell you whose blood this is. Having told you, the record spends no sentence on grief and moves to the arrest. The weight is placed on the reader.

chapter.title: Role in the book
chapter.text: Alma 1 supplies the antagonist for the next twenty chapters. The judge who condemns Alma and Amulek at Ammonihah is identified by this killing; the Amalekites build synagogues after the order of the Nehors; a land of the dead is named for the profession. The book's long argument with priestcraft starts with one homicide in the first year of the judges.

applications.title: Ask who is being paid before you argue about what is being taught
applications.text: Nehor's doctrine of universal salvation is stated once. His doctrine about supporting preachers is the one the chapter fights. When a teaching spreads fast, it is worth knowing what it does for the person teaching it.

applications.title: Defend the rule at the moment it protects someone you dislike
applications.text: The record states that the law had no power on any man for his belief in a paragraph about frauds. A principle you only apply to people you approve of is not a principle yet.

applications.title: Answer a bad argument by living the alternative
applications.text: Nobody refutes Nehor after his execution. What ends the chapter is a description of priests going back to work. Some arguments are settled by conduct that cannot be produced on demand.

applications.title: Notice what your clothes are doing
applications.text: The chapter tracks pride through apparel three separate times, in three different groups. It is a small, visible, repeatable signal, which is exactly why the record keeps using it.

applications.title: Write your discipline against your own side first
applications.text: The church's strict law governs how its own members treat outsiders, at a moment when the members are the ones being attacked. Rules aimed outward are cheap; the useful one names your own side.

applications.title: Hold the money loosely while there is some
applications.text: They became rich and did not set their hearts on riches, and they gave to the sick and the hungry without first checking whether the person was one of theirs. The test arrives with the prosperity.

applications.title: Let somebody's history be stated and then let it go
applications.text: The record tells you who Gideon was, and then does not use it to make the death mean more. Naming what someone was is sometimes the whole of what you can do.

questions.text: What am I being paid, in money or standing or attention, to keep believing?
Whose approval have I mistaken for confirmation that I am right?
Whose belief am I willing to leave alone even though I think it is false?
What rule have I written for other people that I have not written for myself?
Where am I holding a position above people I am supposed to be serving?
If prosperity arrived this year, what would it show about where my heart already is?
